messages.content: What is the difference between gross yield and net yield?

Gross yield: annual rent ÷ property value × 100. Simple but misleading. Net yield: (annual rent − all costs) ÷ property value × 100. Costs include: management fees (8-12% of rent), maintenance (budget 1% of property value per year), insurance, void periods (budget 4-6 weeks/year), mortgage interest, ground rent/service charge if leasehold. A property yielding 7% gross might yield 3-4% net after costs. Net yield is the only number that matters for cash flow decisions. Always model a stressed scenario: 3 months vacant, major repair needed in year 1.
How do you analyse a commercial real estate deal?

Commercial metrics differ from residential: Net Operating Income (NOI) = gross revenue − operating expenses (excluding debt service). Cap rate = NOI ÷ property value — the yield if purchased cash. Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR) = NOI ÷ annual debt service. Lenders require >1.25x DSCR. Cash-on-cash return = annual cash flow after debt service ÷ cash invested. Commercial leases are triple net (tenant pays rates, insurance, maintenance) or full repairing — read the lease carefully. Anchor tenants drive footfall and co-tenants' viability. Vacancy in commercial is binary — one tenant leaving can destroy cash flow entirely.
How does real estate leverage work?

Leverage: using borrowed money (mortgage) to control a larger asset. £50K deposit on a £200K property = 4:1 leverage. If property rises 10% (£20K), your return on the £50K invested is 40% — not 10%. Leverage amplifies both gains and losses. If property falls 10% (£20K), you've lost 40% of your invested capital. Additionally, rental income must exceed mortgage payments + costs to generate positive cash flow. High leverage + negative cash flow = cash drain that requires continuous capital injection. Optimal leverage depends on yield, interest rate, and risk tolerance.
What is the buy-to-let strategy vs fix-and-flip?

Buy-to-let (BTL): purchase property to rent long-term. Income from rent, return from capital appreciation over time. Lower risk, more passive, requires patience. Fix-and-flip: purchase below market value, renovate, sell for profit. Active, project-management intensive, higher return potential but higher risk (cost overruns, market timing, carrying costs). Tax implications differ: BTL rental income taxed as income, capital gains on sale. Flip profit taxed as income if trading (not capital gains). Hybrid: BRRR (Buy, Refurb, Rent, Refinance, Repeat) — add value through renovation, refinance to extract equity, repeat without deploying fresh capital.
What makes a good real estate investment?

Location fundamentals: proximity to employment centres, quality of schools, transport links, amenity quality, and direction of neighbourhood trajectory (improving vs declining). Financial fundamentals: rental yield (annual rent ÷ purchase price — target 5-8% gross), cash-on-cash return (annual cash flow ÷ cash invested), and equity growth potential. Structural fundamentals: condition of property, age of major systems (roof, boiler, electrics), and planning permission potential. The best investments combine positive cash flow now (income) with capital appreciation over time (equity). Never buy based on hope of appreciation alone.
